plan.title: AP Biology: Cells, Energy & Inheritance
plan.hook: A cell is not a bag of chemicals — its membrane decides what crosses, its enzymes decide how fast, and its alleles decide what the next generation can look like.
objectives: Predict the net direction of osmosis across a selectively permeable membrane from the solute on each side
Explain why an enzyme changes a reaction's rate but not its free-energy difference or equilibrium
Work out genotype and phenotype ratios for an Aa × Aa cross under complete dominance
prerequisites: Basic cell vocabulary: membrane, solute, and allele

sections.heading: A boundary that does useful work
points: A cell membrane is selectively permeable: some things cross, others are trapped
Osmosis is water movement across such a membrane; individual molecules move both ways
With equal initial pressure, net water movement is toward the side with more trapped solute

sections.heading: Lower the barrier, keep the destination
points: An enzyme supplies a pathway with a lower activation barrier, so the reaction rate increases
Reactant and product energies are unchanged by catalysis
Catalysis changes neither the overall free-energy difference nor the equilibrium

sections.heading: Count alleles before predicting traits
points: In an Aa × Aa cross the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa
The genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
With complete dominance, AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype, giving a 3:1 phenotype ratio — a probability, not a quota

sections.heading: A boundary that does useful work
sections.body: A cell membrane is selectively permeable. Osmosis is water movement across a selectively permeable membrane. With equal initial pressure, water tends to move toward the side with more solute that cannot cross.
sections.visual: More water crosses toward the side with more trapped solute. Individual water molecules move both ways; the larger arrow shows net movement before pressure balances it.

questions.q: If both sides of a membrane start at equal pressure, which way does water move on balance?
questions.hint: Compare the amount of solute that cannot cross on each side.
questions.answer: Net movement is toward the side with more solute that cannot cross. Individual water molecules move both ways; the net flow goes toward the more trapped solute until pressure balances it.

questions.q: What does it mean that the membrane is selectively permeable?
questions.hint: Think about which substances are allowed through and which are held back.
questions.answer: Some substances can cross the membrane while others cannot. In the osmosis example, water crosses but the solute stays put.

sections.heading: Lower the barrier, keep the destination
sections.body: An enzyme supplies a pathway with a lower activation barrier, increasing reaction rate. Catalysis does not change overall free-energy difference or equilibrium.
sections.visual: The enzyme provides a route with a lower activation-energy barrier. Reactant and product energies stay the same.

questions.q: What does an enzyme actually change about a reaction?
questions.hint: Separate the height of the barrier from the energies of the start and end points.
questions.answer: It supplies a pathway with a lower activation barrier, which increases the reaction rate. It does not change the overall free-energy difference or the equilibrium.

questions.q: Do the reactant and product energies move when an enzyme is added?
questions.hint: Check the visual: which parts of the energy diagram stay put?
questions.answer: No. Reactant and product energies stay the same; only the barrier between them is lower on the enzyme's route.

sections.visual: Each cell combines one allele from each parent. The genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. With complete dominance, three of the four outcomes have the dominant phenotype.

questions.q: Why do AA and Aa look the same in this cross?
questions.hint: The section assumes a particular dominance relationship.
questions.answer: Under complete dominance, one dominant allele is enough to show the dominant phenotype, so AA and Aa share it. Only aa shows the recessive phenotype.

questions.q: A family of four offspring from Aa × Aa are all aa. Has the 3:1 prediction failed?
questions.hint: The diagram calls the ratios probabilities, not quotas.
questions.answer: No. The 3:1 ratio is a probability over many offspring; small families need not match it, and an all-recessive run of four is possible.

questions.q: Two sides of a selectively permeable membrane start at equal pressure. The right side holds more solute that cannot cross. What is the net movement of water?
choices: Toward the right, the side with more trapped solute
Toward the left, away from the solute
No net movement, because water molecules move both ways
Toward whichever side has less water pressure building up
questions.explain: Individual water molecules cross both ways, but with equal initial pressure the net movement is toward the side with more solute that cannot cross, until pressure balances it.

questions.q: In this section's osmosis setup, which substance is the one held back by the membrane?
choices: Water
The solute that cannot cross
Neither — everything crosses freely
Both water and solute
questions.explain: The membrane is selectively permeable: water crosses, while the solute that cannot cross stays trapped on its side — that trapped solute is what drives the net flow.

questions.q: An enzyme speeds up a reaction mainly by…
choices: Lowering the energy of the products
Raising the energy of the reactants
Supplying a pathway with a lower activation barrier
Shifting the equilibrium toward the products
questions.explain: The enzyme's route has a lower activation-energy barrier, so the rate increases. Reactant and product energies — and therefore the free-energy difference and equilibrium — stay the same.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium will…
choices: Move the equilibrium toward the products
Move the equilibrium toward the reactants
Leave the equilibrium unchanged
Change the overall free-energy difference
questions.explain: Catalysis does not change the overall free-energy difference or equilibrium. It only lowers the barrier, so equilibrium is reached faster, not in a different place.

questions.q: For an Aa × Aa cross with complete dominance, what are the expected genotype and phenotype ratios?
choices: Genotypes 3:1, phenotypes 1:2:1
Genotypes 1:2:1, phenotypes 3:1
Genotypes 1:1, phenotypes 1:1
Genotypes 1:2:1, phenotypes 1:2:1
questions.explain: The four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa — a 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa genotype ratio. With complete dominance AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype, so phenotypes run 3:1.

questions.q: The 3:1 phenotype ratio from an Aa × Aa cross is best described as…
choices: A guaranteed count in every set of four offspring
A probability that small families need not match
A ratio that applies only to the first four offspring
A pattern that holds only when no aa offspring appear
questions.explain: The diagram states it directly: ratios are probabilities, and small families need not match them. The 3:1 emerges over many offspring, not as a quota per family.

sections.title: Water follows the trapped solute
bullets: The membrane is selectively permeable: water crosses, some solute cannot.
Individual water molecules move both ways across the membrane.
Net movement runs toward the side with more trapped solute until pressure balances.
sections.notes: Picture two compartments split by a membrane that lets water through but not the solute. Molecules cross in both directions, yet the balance of movement favours the side with more trapped solute — that imbalance is osmosis.
sections.visual: More water crosses toward the side with more trapped solute. Individual water molecules move both ways; the larger arrow shows net movement before pressure balances it.

sections.title: Lower barrier, same destination
bullets: An enzyme offers a route with a lower activation-energy barrier.
A lower barrier means a faster reaction rate.
Free-energy difference and equilibrium are exactly where they were without the enzyme.
sections.notes: The enzyme does not move the start or finish lines of the energy diagram. It cuts a lower pass through the hill between them, so more molecules get over per second — but where the reaction settles is unchanged.
sections.visual: The enzyme provides a route with a lower activation-energy barrier. Reactant and product energies stay the same.

sections.title: Count alleles before phenotypes
bullets: Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, aA, aa with equal likelihood.
Complete dominance merges AA and Aa into one phenotype: 3:1.
Ratios are probabilities — small families need not match.
sections.notes: Each parent contributes one allele per offspring, so four combinations are equally likely. Count genotypes first (1:2:1), then apply complete dominance to get phenotypes (3:1) — and remember these are odds, not quotas.
sections.visual: Each cell combines one allele from each parent. The genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. With complete dominance, three of the four outcomes have the dominant phenotype.

enrichment.audioTitle: AP Biology: Cells, Energy & Inheritance — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Three ideas run this course: a membrane that chooses what crosses, an enzyme that lowers a barrier, and a cross you can count. Start with the membrane — what does selectively permeable mean?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: That it lets some substances through and keeps others out?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly. In osmosis, water crosses but a solute cannot. If both sides start at equal pressure and one side has more of that trapped solute, which way does water move on balance?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Water molecules move both ways, so maybe there is no net movement?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: The molecules do move both ways — but not equally. Net movement is toward the side with more trapped solute, and it continues until pressure balances it.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: So osmosis is about the net flow, not each molecule.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Right. Now the enzyme section. Its heading says "lower the barrier, keep the destination." What is the destination that stays put?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: The equilibrium? And the free-energy difference?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Both. The enzyme supplies a pathway with a lower activation barrier, so the rate rises — but reactant and product energies are unchanged, so the free-energy difference and equilibrium stay where they were.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: I used to think enzymes pushed reactions toward products. They just get there faster.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That is the correction to keep. Last section: Aa × Aa. What are the four equally likely combinations?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: AA, Aa, aA and aa — so genotypes run 1:2:1.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: And with complete dominance, what do phenotypes do?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: AA and Aa look the same, so it is 3:1 dominant to recessive.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Yes. One warning from the diagram: those ratios are probabilities. A small family of four need not show 3:1 — what would you say to someone who calls that a failed prediction?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: That the ratio describes odds over many offspring, not a quota every family of four must fill.

nodes.note: Catalysis changes neither the free-energy difference nor the equilibrium position.
